scenes.heading: Factorising monic quadratics
scenes.sub: Turn x² + 8x + 15 back into two brackets
scenes.say: Expanding turns brackets into a long expression. Factorising goes the other way. In this video you will learn to turn quadratics like x squared plus eight x plus fifteen back into two brackets, every time.
scenes.caption: Expanding turns brackets into a long expression. Factorising goes the other way. In this video you will learn to turn quadratics like x² + 8x + 15 back into two brackets, every time.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Arrange 1 big tile, 8 strips and 15 small squares into a rectangle
scenes.breaks: You can't hold a negative tile, so for negative terms you need sign rules instead.
scenes.say: Imagine one big square tile, eight long strips and fifteen small squares. Can you arrange them into a rectangle? Three strips one way, five the other, and the fifteen small squares fill the corner. The rectangle's sides are x plus three and x plus five. Factorising means finding those sides.

scenes.heading: The area model
scenes.say: Here is the rectangle. First the big x squared tile, then the strips, three x and five x, then the corner of fifteen. The corner is the product of the two numbers, and the strips add to the middle term. So we need two numbers that multiply to fifteen and add to eight.
scenes.caption: First the x² tile, then the strips 3x and 5x, then the corner 15. The corner is the product; the strips add to the middle term. So we need two numbers that multiply to 15 and add to 8.

scenes.heading: Sign clues
points: c positive, b positive: both numbers positive
c positive, b negative: both numbers negative
c negative: one positive, one negative
Take out any common factor or −1 first
scenes.say: The signs give you clues. If the constant is positive, both numbers have the same sign as the middle term. If the constant is negative, the signs are different. And always take out a common factor first, including minus one if the x squared term is negative.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Factorise fully 2x² − 16x + 30.
scenes.say: Factorise two x squared minus sixteen x plus thirty. First take out the common factor two. Inside, find two numbers that multiply to fifteen and add to negative eight. That's negative three and negative five. Keep the two at the front.
scenes.caption: Factorise 2x² − 16x + 30. Take out 2: 2(x² − 8x + 15). Multiply to 15, add to −8: −3 and −5. Answer: 2(x − 3)(x − 5).

scenes.heading: A hidden quadratic
scenes.question: Factorise fully x⁴ − 13x² + 36.
scenes.say: Here's a challenge. x to the four minus thirteen x squared plus thirty-six is a quadratic in disguise. Let u equal x squared. Now it's u squared minus thirteen u plus thirty-six, which is u minus four times u minus nine. Put x squared back, then split each difference of two squares.
scenes.caption: x⁴ − 13x² + 36 is a quadratic in disguise. Let u = x²: u² − 13u + 36 = (u − 4)(u − 9). Put x² back, then split each difference of two squares.

points: Multiply to c, add to b
scenes.say: Quick recap. Take out any common factor first. Find two numbers that multiply to the constant and add to the middle coefficient. Use the signs as clues, spot the special patterns, and always expand to check. Now try the practice questions!
